title: Connecting AI to External Tools
learning_outcomes: Explain connecting AI to External Tools and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.
Apply the central idea in connecting AI to External Tools to a small example or select a suitable approach for a stated scenario.
Identify an important assumption, failure mode, risk, or limitation and describe how it should be checked.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study connecting AI to External Tools within Building Applications with Large Language Models. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: An AI application includes much more than a model call: data flow, validation, retrieval, access control, observability, and failure handling matter.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Tool use connects model-selected actions to functions controlled by application code. Validate arguments, enforce server-side authorization, restrict permissions, and verify tool results before performing any consequential action.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: Tool definitions and schemas
items.text: Tool definitions and schemas is one of the concepts used to reason about connecting ai to external tools. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Function calling
items.text: Tool use lets a model request a defined operation, but the application should validate parameters and authorize the operation independently. Treat the model’s proposed action as untrusted input.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Identify what connecting ai to external tools takes as input and what result or decision it is intended to support. 2. Read the example before running it and predict the output. 3. Run the small example, compare actual and expected output, then change one input or assumption and repeat. 4. Record what the example demonstrates and what it does not demonstrate about a real system.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with the task definition and the inputs available. Make the expected behavior explicit, choose a simple reference point, and inspect both ordinary examples and cases where assumptions may fail. An AI application includes much more than a model call: data flow, validation, retrieval, access control, observability, and failure handling matter.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Copy the code into a local file named main.py and run `python main.py` with Python 3. Compare the printed output with the expected result documented here. This CodeLeaf content block is static; it does not execute the snippet in the browser and needs no external API key.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet or return to the small synthetic input, rerun it, and change one value at a time. Do not add real credentials, private user data, or untrusted code to the example.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Tool use connects model-selected actions to functions controlled by application code. Validate arguments, enforce server-side authorization, restrict permissions, and verify tool results before performing any consequential action. Next, connect this lesson to its prerequisite or next lesson and carry the same habit forward: define success, test a representative case, inspect failures, and document limitations.

content.task: Try it yourself: sketch a small application for connecting ai to external tools with explicit inputs, outputs, and a failure path. Use a mock response rather than a live API key; validate output structure and test at least one unsupported or malformed case.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core concept and accurately refer to the source syllabus topics.
Record a prediction and compare it with a reproducible result or a clearly stated manual trace.
Document at least one limitation, safety consideration, or evaluation requirement.
hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
